# Chapter One

The roar was everything. It filled the narrow mountain pass with sound so complete that the world became only noise and light and the taste of burnt stone on the tongue. The lightning had struck the old pine where it stood on the exposed ridge, and the bolt came not once but in a chain, each flash searing away another layer of bark and resin in a smell like burning hair and altar incense. The man's hands were locked around the trunk. His palms pressed flat against the wood, skin already blackening where the electricity had found its path through him and into the earth. He should have let go. Everything in the body screams to release, to fall away, to survive. But his fingers curled deeper into the fissures the lightning had opened, and when the final bolt came, it was almost gentle. The sound cut out. The light collapsed into purple and then nothing.

He fell backward onto the scree. His palms faced upward, scored and blistered, the skin already beginning to char at the edges where the current had exited his body into the stone beneath him. The storm was moving, the rain suddenly cold and ordinary. Around him the pass lay quiet. The old pine tree still stood, smoking.

The world tilted. For a moment there was no time at all.

Then the mountains were different. The light was wrong. The storm was gone, and two hundred years had passed.

Luca stood at the edge of the clearing where Italus should have been, and the earth beneath his feet told a story he could not yet read. The pine was gone. Not fallen, not dead. Gone. The ground around the old root cavity was soft and recently disturbed, the soil darker where it had been turned. Broken root ends protruded from the exposed bank like pale fingers, still raw where they had torn free. His heart moved into his throat in a way that made him dizzy.

He had been coming to this place since early spring, when the winter snow began to pull back from the high meadows. Always under some excuse, always with a reason that had seemed sufficient at the time. He was tracking a missing lamb that had wandered higher than the herds normally went. He was searching for the rare alpine herbs his mother had asked him to find. He was exploring a new route for the spring migration. Each excuse had worked once, perhaps twice. Now, in the late summer, with the shepherd's work pressing from dawn until dusk, his repeated absences had begun to draw attention he did not want.

His father had noticed first. The old man had not said anything directly, only watched Luca with a particular kind of stillness as he saddled his horse before dawn, the way fathers watch when they are trying to determine whether their sons are becoming men or fools. His mother had asked more questions. Where exactly was he going? How long would he be gone? What was worth spending so much time in the high country when there was work to be done? The other shepherds had begun to joke about it. Even his younger cousin Marco had started to follow him sometimes, curious about where Luca disappeared to, what he was doing alone in the Pollino heights where nothing of real value grew.

The village priest had asked him directly after mass one Sunday, his voice casual but his eyes sharp. Was there something troubling the boy's conscience? Was he perhaps meeting someone he should not be meeting? The question had been phrased as concern, but Luca had felt the trap in it. One truthful answer would have led to more questions, to suspicion, to scrutiny of a kind that would have made it impossible to keep coming back here.

So he had lied. Small lies first, the easiest ones. He had said nothing at all, which was a kind of lie. Then as the questions had grown more insistent, he had invented details. There was a shepherd's shelter that had been damaged in a winter storm, and he was repairing it. There was a marking post that needed replacing. He was following the high ridgeline to check for new snow damage or rock falls. Each lie had felt like a stone added to a cairn, and the cairn was growing heavier.

Luca knelt at the edge of the disturbed ground and ran his fingers along the scored earth. The disturbance was recent, maybe days old. The exposed soil still held moisture. He could see the pattern of whatever had moved through here, a direction and a force. The roots had been torn downward and outward, as if Italus had been pulled from the earth with tremendous strength, as if the tree had been wrenched up from the ground against its own weight and resistance.

That was impossible. Italus had stood in this meadow for at least as long as Luca's grandfather had been alive, probably longer. The tree was thick as a man's torso and twice his height. It would have taken a team of strong men and tools to fell it, and there were no marks of an axe, no sawdust, no evidence of any human labor at all. Only the torn earth and the scattered stones that had been displaced by the root-ball as it was lifted.

Luca's throat tightened. He stood up and walked the perimeter of the disturbance, trying to understand the geometry of what had happened here. The uprooted space was large, perhaps four paces across. The soil around it was compacted in places and loose in others, scuffed and churned in a pattern that suggested violence or panic. He could see where something heavy had been dragged away from the center point. A trail of broken vegetation and upturned stones led downslope toward the higher meadows, fading as the ground grew harder and the grass thicker.

He followed it for perhaps fifty paces before he lost the trail entirely. The afternoon light was beginning to change, the sun dropping behind the far ridge, and he knew he should be returning to his flock. His father would be wondering where he was. There would be more questions, more excuses to manufacture, more lies to add to the cairn.

But something made him stop. A feeling rather than a thought, a sense of being observed. He turned slowly, looking back at the clearing and then out across the surrounding meadows. The mountains around Pollino held many secrets. There were caves in the upper reaches, and old hermitages built by monks who had wanted to be alone with God and silence. There were shepherds from villages too distant to be known, hunters who came up in the autumn, travelers who took the high passes to avoid the roads below.

There was also a man standing at the edge of the pine grove about a hundred paces away, motionless in the shadows.

Luca's first instinct was to run. His second was to freeze. Neither seemed quite right, and so he did neither, only straightened and turned fully to face the figure. The man did not move. He was tall and lean, wearing dark clothes that seemed to absorb the failing light. There was something about his stillness that suggested long practice, a deliberate and careful patience. He was watching Luca with the focus of something that had been waiting for a very long time.

Luca took a step backward, not fleeing but creating distance. The man made no move toward him. He only stood and watched. After perhaps thirty seconds, a time that felt very long, the man turned and walked slowly back into the trees. He did not look hurried or frightened. He moved like someone leaving a place he had already decided to leave, taking his time, making no fuss about it.

Luca waited until the figure had disappeared completely from view before he turned and began walking back down the mountain. His legs felt strange, disconnected from his will, obeying instructions that came from somewhere deeper than thought. The sun was sinking faster now, painting the western sky in shades of red and copper. By the time he reached the lower meadows where his sheep were grazing, the stars were beginning to emerge.

Over the next two weeks, Luca returned to the clearing five times. Each time he found the trail of the uprooted tree leading deeper into the high country. Each time he followed it for a distance before giving up, the trail fragmenting into smaller branches that could have been made by deer or falling rocks or his own imagination. The compacted area around the old root cavity was slowly being reclaimed by the growth of new grass and the work of insects and weather, smoothing the violence of the disturbance into something more natural.

And each time he went, he was aware of being watched.

It was never the same vantage point. Sometimes he felt the observation from the western slope of the ridge, sometimes from deeper in the pine forest, sometimes from a distance so great that it might have been only his own paranoia providing a phantom observer. But the quality of the watching never changed. It was patient and deliberate and wholly without hostility. Someone was keeping track of his visits, his movements, the amount of time he spent searching. Someone was learning his patterns.

His family noticed. His father said nothing, but the quality of his silence changed. His mother began to ask more pointed questions about his excuses. She wanted to know if he had a girl in the high country, if there was something he was ashamed of, if his behavior was signaling some kind of trouble that required attention. She suggested, gently at first and then less gently, that perhaps the mountain air was affecting him, that perhaps he should spend more time with the other young people of the village instead of disappearing into the heights alone.

Marco followed him again and reported back that Luca had been "just wandering around that one meadow like he'd lost something," which was accurate enough to be dangerous. The other shepherds had begun to make jokes that were less friendly than before, suggesting that Luca was too soft for real work, that he was becoming strange, that he preferred the company of the rocks to the company of men.

By late August, his absences had become the subject of conversations he was not part of. He could feel the weight of those conversations in the way his parents looked at him, in the careful distance his father maintained, in the new caution his mother brought to her questions. In another few weeks, someone would likely decide that the matter required direct intervention. His father might forbid him from going to the heights. His mother might insist on taking him to see the priest. Marco or one of the other shepherds might follow him more aggressively, determined to solve the mystery.

He needed a better excuse. Something with the authority of tradition, something that could not be easily questioned. Something that would make his repeated journeys to the Pollino heights seem not suspicious but pious.

It was late afternoon when he first saw the monk on the trail.

Luca had taken what seemed like a more direct route from the village, hoping to reach the clearing before the light failed completely. The path wound through a stand of birch trees where the stones were more stable underfoot, and it was narrow enough that only one person could pass at a time. The monk was standing in the middle of the path about twenty paces ahead, as if he had been waiting for Luca to arrive, though there was no way he could have known Luca was coming.

He was a small man, compact and wiry, with gray hair worn cropped close to his skull. His robes were brown and worn, patched in several places with material that did not quite match. His feet were bare, calloused and darkened by exposure to sun and stone. His hands hung at his sides, and Luca noticed without wanting to that the palms were marked with old scars that looked like burns.

"You come to these heights often," the monk said. It was not a question. His voice was rough, as if it did not get much use, and his accent was not from any village Luca knew.

Luca stopped walking. His instinct was to deny it, to claim that this was only his second or third time in the high country, but something about the monk's stillness made lying seem pointless. "Sometimes," he said.

"Your family does not know where you go."

It was another statement of fact rather than an inquiry. Luca said nothing.

The monk stepped to the side of the path, making space. "Come. Walk with me."

Luca did not move. He was fourteen years old and not particularly large for his age, and the monk was old and small. In theory, Luca could have tried to push past him or to run back down the trail. But something in the monk's bearing suggested that physical resistance would be ineffective, and that trying would be an embarrassment.

"Your visits are becoming noticed," the monk said, continuing as if Luca had agreed to walk with him. "Another week or two and your absence will become the subject of serious concern. Your mother will want to know the truth. Your father will want to know the truth. Perhaps they will decide to forbid you from coming."

"I'm only exploring," Luca said. It sounded thin even to himself.

"You are searching for something that cannot be found through ordinary means," the monk said. "Your family will not understand that. They will assume you are troubled or hiding a secret that shames you. They will want to fix what they perceive as broken. And you will lose the freedom to come to these heights at all."

Luca felt something settle in his chest, a recognition that this stranger had understood something true about his situation. "What do you want?" he asked.

"To offer you an alternative explanation for your visits," the monk said. "A reason that is socially acceptable and that your family cannot reasonably dispute."

"What explanation?"

"Prayer," the monk said simply. "You come to these heights to pray. To be alone with God. It is a reasonable thing for a young man to do, particularly a young man who may be beginning to feel the call of a contemplative life. Your family cannot argue with that motivation. The priest cannot argue with it. The village cannot argue with it."

Luca considered this. "I don't know how to pray," he said.

"Then you will learn," the monk said. "I can teach you. I live in the high country in a small hermitage not far from here. If you come regularly to study the practice of prayer, if you can speak of it to your family with a proper degree of seriousness, then your visits will be accepted. Perhaps even approved."

"Why would you do that?" Luca asked.

The monk was quiet for a long moment. When he spoke again, his voice was even rougher than before, as if the question had cost him something. "Because I was young once, and I had things I needed to protect that no one could know about. And because sometimes an older person has learned enough to help a younger person avoid the mistakes of secrecy and isolation."

"Who are you?" Luca asked.

The monk smiled, a small and private expression. "My name is not important. I am a hermit monk who lives in these mountains and seeks solitude. That is all anyone needs to know. If you tell your family that you have met me, you can tell them that I have offered to teach you the practices of prayer. They will accept that. And you will be free to continue your work here."

"Work," Luca repeated. He had not thought of it as work before, this searching and learning and watching. But that was what it was, he realized. It was work.

"Yes," the monk said. "Work. I suspect you understand that now better than most people your age would. But you still have much to learn about how to do it safely, how to keep yourself and your purpose protected from scrutiny. I can help you with that."

Luca said nothing. He was thinking of the feeling of being watched, the sense of a patient observer tracking his movements. He was thinking of the torn earth in the clearing, the impossible uprooting, the trail that led deeper into the mountains toward places he had not yet explored.

He was thinking of the person who was clearly following him, who clearly knew something about what had happened to Italus, and who was offering him not answers but protection.

"All right," Luca said. "Teach me to pray."

The monk nodded once, as if this was what he had expected. "Come to the clearing at dawn tomorrow. I will show you the first things. And when you return to your village, you tell your family that you have begun studying the contemplative life. You say it with conviction and seriousness. You make it sound like something important has changed in you. They want to believe that you are becoming a serious person. Give them that narrative, and they will accept your absences."

"What if they ask more questions?"

"Then you tell them the truth about prayer. You tell them about the things you are learning. You do not tell them about me, specifically. You tell them about learning from a hermit teacher. That is not a lie. You simply do not provide the details of who I am or what I look like. Do you understand?"

Luca understood. It was a subtle thing, the difference between lying and incomplete truth, but it was a distinction he could work with.

"One more thing," the monk said. He reached out and took Luca's left hand, turning the palm upward. "Keep this safe. This work that you are doing, whatever it is that you are protecting, it will require sacrifice. But the sacrifice will not be your body or your freedom if you are careful. The sacrifice will be small and ongoing. You will give up the comfort of honesty with your family. You will give up the simplicity of a normal life. But you will keep your autonomy. And that is worth protecting."

He released Luca's hand, and the boy pulled it back. It was an odd blessing or warning, and Luca was not sure which.

The monk turned and began walking up the trail, toward the higher meadows and the clearing beyond. After a few paces, he called back over his shoulder, "At dawn. Do not be late. I do not have much time for distractions."

Then he was gone, moving into the shadows between the birch trees with a speed that seemed impossible for someone of his age and size.

Luca stood in the failing light and tried to process what had just happened. The stranger knew about his visits. The stranger was offering him cover, a socially acceptable reason for his absences. The stranger seemed to know exactly what Luca needed and was offering to provide it. And the stranger had those scars on his palms, old scars that looked like burns.

In the weeks that followed, Luca did exactly as the monk had instructed. He went home and told his parents that he had met a hermit teacher in the mountains who was offering to instruct him in the practices of contemplative prayer and monastic discipline. He said it with as much seriousness as he could manage. He spoke about feeling called to understand his faith more deeply, about wanting to learn the tools for a spiritual life, about the value of solitude and reflection.

His mother seemed relieved to have an explanation for his behavior that made sense within the framework of acceptable religious devotion. His father, after some deliberation, decided that this was not a shameful thing and that a young man could certainly do worse than to seek spiritual instruction. The other shepherds seemed to lose interest once Luca began talking openly about his prayers and his studies. The village priest, when Luca mentioned it to him in confession, offered his approval and even some basic instruction of his own, though he seemed somewhat surprised that Luca preferred to study with a hermit rather than under his direct guidance.

By late August, Luca's repeated absences had been transformed from suspicious to pious. His family still knew he was going to the heights, but they understood why now, or thought they did. The scrutiny eased. The questions became fewer and less suspicious. Marco stopped trying to follow him because there was nothing mysterious about a young man pursuing his spiritual development.

And with that protection in place, with his cover secure and his freedom assured, Luca could finally commit fully to the work that had drawn him to the clearing in the first place.

He did not yet understand what Italus was, or how a tree had been torn from the earth and moved through these mountains. He did not understand why the monk was so invested in his protection, or what the scars on those old palms signified. He did not know what the next steps would be or how long this path would take to walk.

But he understood now that he was a guardian of something. And he understood that to be a guardian effectively, he had to learn to hide that guardianship in plain sight. The monk had taught him the first and most essential skill: how to protect what mattered by making it invisible through the lens of acceptable social behavior.

It was a small magic, but it was powerful. And as Luca walked back down the mountain in the full darkness, the stars bright enough to navigate by, he felt something settle into place inside him that had been restless and uncertain before.

He had a purpose now. And he had the beginning of the tools to protect it.
